title: The poem and Gibb's text
short: Ghazel [8] in Gibb (1900): an invitation to a friend to take up the mystic path together and seek God, the 'Loved One'.
body: Gibb printed this short ghazel after the two 'pantheistic' poems, describing it as apparently an invitation to some friend to follow the mystic life. His notes gloss 'the Loved One' and 'the Friend' as God, and 'the lover' as the mystic. Where the preceding poem speaks with God's voice, this one is human and companionable, the voice of a dervish urging a fellow traveller. Such poems were sung as hymns (ilahi) in the Sufi lodges of Anatolia and the Balkans, which is how Yunus's verse spread from the fourteenth century on, according to Tatcı. Gibb translated from the Divan lithographed in 1884-5; he does not print the Turkish, and attributions in that Divan are not all secure.

anchor: let us seek the Loved One
title: The refrain
short: Every couplet ends with the same summons, so the poem works as a sung hymn with a refrain the congregation can carry.
body: Each of the six couplets closes with 'come and let us seek the Loved One', Gibb's rendering of a repeated end-phrase (redif). Gibb's preface explains that he imitates the rhyme pattern and, where he can, the syllable count of his originals; his line is a long trochaic one of sixteen syllables in two halves of eight, which suggests the long syllabic lines of Turkish folk verse, though Gibb gives no Turkish text to confirm it. Gibb held that Yunus wrote only in native syllabic metres; the modern editor Mustafa Tatcı counts some 138 of 417 poems in the Persian quantitative metre (aruz), so the point needs checking against the original. The refrain suits communal singing in the dervish lodge.

title: 'guide me on our faring'
short: The mystic life as a journey on a road (yol, tarikat) under a guide; 'faring' is the old word for travelling.
body: 'Faring' (OED, from 'fare', to go or travel) keeps the old sense of a journey. The journey is the Sufi Path (Arabic tariqa, Turkish tarikat or simply yol), which the seeker walks in stages under a spiritual guide (mürşid). Yunus himself had such a guide, Tapduk Emre, whose disciple he was, according to the Ottoman biographers Gibb summarises. Here the roles are shared: the speaker asks the friend to guide him, and both walk together. The image of the road and the travelling companion (yoldaş, 'road-mate') is basic to Anatolian dervish poetry.

title: Internal rhyme: faring, repairing, caring
short: Three chiming rhymes inside the couplet before the refrain: Gibb's imitation of the Turkish internal sub-rhyme he finds in most of Yunus's ghazels.
body: The second couplet rhymes 'faring', 'repairing', 'caring' within the lines and then returns to the refrain; couplets 3 and 5 do the same (together / wither / never; impel us / hail us / assail us). Gibb notes that most of Yunus's ghazels use the favourite Turkish arrangement of a thrice-repeated internal sub-rhyme, in practice the same as the stanza-like form learned poets called musammat, and that Yunus's rhymes are often only assonant. Gibb's English copies this, including the near-rhymes. 'Repairing' means going to a place, as in 'repair to the court' (OED, repair v.1), not mending.

title: 'the Friend'
short: Gibb glosses 'the Friend' as God: Dost is one of the commonest names for God in Turkish mystical poetry.
body: Gibb's note says simply that 'the Friend' is God. The Persian word dost, Turkish dost, is a standard name for God in Sufi poetry, alongside the Beloved (yâr, maşuk) and the Truth (Hak); Yunus uses it constantly. The term turns religion into a relationship of love and intimacy rather than fear: the seeker goes to God as to a friend's house. It also links the two friendships in the poem, the human comradeship of the two travellers and their shared love for the divine Friend.

title: 'dule'
greek: Old French doel, Latin dolus / dolor ('grief')
short: 'Dule' is an old Scots and northern spelling of 'dole', grief or sorrow; with 'caring' it means worldly sorrow and anxiety.
body: 'Dule' (OED, under dole n.2, 'grief, sorrow', of which dule is a Scots and northern form) belongs to the archaic diction Gibb uses to give his versions an antique, ballad-like flavour, here no doubt also for the rhyme. 'Dule and caring' means grief and worldly anxiety: the cares that bind the soul to the world. In Sufi teaching the seeker must cast them off, because sorrow over what passes is itself a form of attachment; the only grief the lover keeps is longing for the Friend.

anchor: Let us quit the world together
title: Leaving the world
greek: Arabic dunyā ('the near, the lower world'); Turkish dünya
short: Renunciation of the world, which deceives and withers; the Qur'an calls worldly life 'the enjoyment of delusion'.
body: 'Quit the world' means renunciation (Arabic zuhd, the first stage of the Path), not literal flight: the seeker detaches the heart from wealth, rank and pleasure. 'Cheated not' means 'not deceived by it', since the world is a cheat: the Qur'an calls the life of this world 'the enjoyment of delusion' (mata' al-ghurur, Q 57:20), and in the same verse compares it to vegetation that flourishes and then withers into straw, the image behind 'for it doth wither'. The couplet's last line, 'Let us two be parted never', turns renunciation into a pledge of companionship: what the two friends give up they replace with each other and with God.

title: 'Soothly is the world unstable'
short: 'Soothly' means 'truly': the world is transient (fâni), a central theme of Yunus and of Turkish devotional verse.
body: 'Soothly' is the archaic adverb 'truly' (OED, from sooth, 'truth'). The idea that the world is fleeting (Turkish fâni dünya) is perhaps the most persistent theme of Yunus's poetry and of the Turkish hymns derived from it, rooted in the Qur'an's 'All that is on earth will perish, and there remains the face of your Lord' (Q 55:26-7). The world is 'unstable' in two senses: it changes, and it gives no firm footing to anyone who leans on it. The theme sets up the warnings of death in couplet 5.

title: The sleeping soul
short: Heedlessness as sleep: a famous saying, 'People are asleep; when they die they wake', attributed to the Prophet and to 'Ali.
body: Sufi teachers called the state of the worldly soul ghafla, Turkish gaflet, heedlessness or forgetfulness of God, and pictured it as sleep. The best-known form is the saying 'People are asleep, and when they die they wake up', often quoted as a saying of the Prophet and also reported as a saying of 'Ali; Mohammed Rustom has studied Mulla Sadra's commentary on it. Yunus's line urges the friend to wake now, before death forces the awakening. 'Ope' is the archaic short form of 'open'.

title: 'fere'
short: 'Fere' is an archaic word for a companion or mate, literally a fellow-traveller (Old English gefera).
body: 'Fere' (OED, fere n.1) is an old word for a companion, comrade or spouse, from Old English gefera, one who goes (faran) with another: a fellow traveller, exactly the Turkish yoldaş, 'road-companion'. It survives mainly in ballads and in Burns's 'Auld Lang Syne' ('my trusty fiere'). Gibb's 'fere and comrade' doubles the idea, as Yunus doubles 'comrades' and 'helpmates' in the opening couplet. The repetition shows that the poem is as much about friendship on the Path as about the goal.

title: Fate and Death
short: Three warnings in one couplet: before Fate seizes us, before Death calls, before the Angel of Death attacks, set out now.
body: The fifth couplet builds a triple 'ere' (before) clause, each rhyming internally (impel us, hail us, assail us), and so turns the invitation into an urgent memento mori. 'Fate' probably stands for the appointed hour of death (Turkish ecel, from Arabic ajal), which the Qur'an says can be neither delayed nor hastened (Q 7:34); 'the voice of Death' that 'hails' is the summons no one can refuse. The climax, the Angel of Death himself, gives the abstract terms a face. The urgency is typical of Yunus, whose poems on death and the grave are among his most famous.

title: 'Azra'il
short: Gibb: 'Azra'il is the name of the Angel of Death, who takes each soul at its appointed time.
body: Gibb's note identifies 'Azra'il as the Angel of Death. The Qur'an speaks of 'the angel of death who has been put in charge of you' (Q 32:11) without naming him; the name 'Azra'il, probably of Hebrew origin, comes from later tradition. In Turkish he is Azrail, a familiar and dreaded figure of popular religion and folk poetry: Chodzko's note to one of the Köroğlu songs in this archive calls him 'Ezrael'. Yunus's line pictures him as an assailant, the one who strikes when the term of life runs out.

title: The lover
short: Gibb: 'the lover is of course the mystic'. Âşık, the lover of God, is Yunus's name for the true seeker.
body: Gibb's note: 'the lover' is the mystic. Arabic 'ashiq, Turkish âşık, is the key word of Yunus's poetry, the one who loves God with a passion that consumes the self, as opposed to the zâhid, the cold ascetic. The same word later named the wandering minstrel-poets of Anatolia (âşık), who sang Köroğlu's songs among others; Chodzko records the northern Persian form for professional singers. 'Loyal' stresses fidelity: the true lover keeps faith in spite of suffering. The couplet asks that the two friends find such a lover to bring them news ('tidings') of the Truth.

title: 'The Truth'
short: 'The Truth' (Hak) is God, the Real; the lover brings news of Him as a messenger brings news of a distant beloved.
body: Gibb's capitals mark 'The Truth' as a divine Name, Arabic al-Haqq, Turkish Hak, the commonest name for God in Yunus. 'Tidings' casts the lover as a messenger who has been where the Beloved is and can report on Him, a familiar device of love poetry, where the lover waits for news of the absent beloved. The search for 'the Loved One' is thus partly a search for the right human guide, the true lover who already knows the way.

title: The signature: 'the lover Yunus'
short: Yunus names himself in the last couplet; the friends are to seek out Yunus, the lover. Other poets, notably Âşık Yunus, also signed this way.
body: As in the ghazel convention, the poet's name appears in the last couplet. Here the speaker seems to step outside himself: 'Let us find the lover Yunus', as if Yunus were the guide the friends should seek. Some readers take this as the humility of a dervish who speaks of himself in the third person; others as a sign that the poem is addressed by Yunus, as teacher, to his disciples. The phrase 'lover Yunus' (âşık Yunus) raises a further problem: the Divan contains poems by a later poet, Âşık Yunus of Bursa (d. early fifteenth century), who signed in the same way, and Tatcı notes that the two have been confused. Gibb, without the modern critical editions, does not discuss the question for this poem.
